speaker: Guillermo Rauch
title: A conversation with Vercel's Guillermo Rauch
question: In AI software platforms, why do pure usage-based or pure seat-based pricing models break down in practice?
guest: For people working on very advanced compiler or cloud infrastructure, there is just not enough data, so AI gives them lower returns today. You need a very fluid model of accounting and billing. When you think about your pricing model and how you monetize—especially if there is an intelligence component or a power component—you need real-time transparency back to your customer. At the same time, SaaS models are still very relevant. There is a lot that is rightfully metered by seat, by project, or by some other unit. So where Vercel exists today is a hybrid world: very much on-demand for compute and intelligence, and more traditional for things related to collaboration and other aspects of building software, like you would pay for GitHub or Figma. Sometimes entrepreneurs get into a cold-start problem, because if you do everything on demand, you may have a hundred thousand customers that pay you three cents a month while you still have fixed platform costs.

points.core: Pure on-demand pricing fails when tiny user spend cannot cover fixed platform costs.
points.note: Accept: cold-start unit economics problem where many low-usage customers pay pennies per month against baseline hosting or infrastructure overhead. Do not credit: generic statements that usage pricing has unpredictable revenue.

points.core: AI usage intensity varies dramatically across seats because specialized domains gain fewer returns.
points.note: Accept: power users running heavy parallel agent sessions versus specialists in frontier or data-scarce domains getting little AI value, making flat per-seat pricing mismatched. Do not credit: vague mentions that different customers have different needs.

points.core: Metered compute billing requires real-time unit-level spend transparency to earn customer trust.
points.note: Accept: showing live accounting of tokens, credits, requests, or compute units as customers consume elastic AI resources. Do not credit: generic advice to be transparent with customers.

points.core: Traditional seat-based subscriptions still fit collaborative platform features better than elastic usage metering.
points.note: Accept: hybrid models pairing recurring seat or project fees for collaboration tools with metered usage for variable AI or compute load. Do not credit: generic claims that SaaS is dead or that hybrid pricing is popular without explaining why.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Both models break because AI decouples the value delivered, the cost to serve, and the number of human users, and each pure model tracks only one of those.

Seat-based pricing fails on two fronts. Costs scale with compute consumed, not headcount, so a flat per-seat fee lets a small group of power users burn through far more inference than they pay for, eroding margins. And as AI automates work, customers need fewer human seats, so the vendor's revenue shrinks precisely as its product becomes more valuable.

Pure usage-based pricing fixes the cost alignment but creates other problems. Customers can't forecast bills, which complicates budgeting and procurement and makes people ration usage, suppressing adoption. Vendors get volatile, hard-to-predict revenue. And units like tokens or credits measure activity rather than outcomes, so they are opaque to buyers and face steady price pressure as underlying model costs fall.

That's why most platforms converge on hybrids: a base subscription or seat fee for predictability, bundled usage allowances or credits, and overage or outcome-based charges for heavy consumption.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Pure seat-based pricing breaks down in AI software because it decouples revenue from both underlying costs and delivered value. Unlike traditional SaaS with near-zero marginal costs, AI platforms incur variable compute expenses on every action; a single power user or background agent can consume massive inference resources on one seat and erode gross margins. Worse, as AI automates workflows and boosts productivity, customers often need fewer human operators—meaning seat revenue paradoxically shrinks the more value the software delivers.

Pure usage-based pricing protects vendor margins by metering tokens or compute, but fails on predictability and incentive alignment. Enterprise buyers demand budget certainty, and uncapped variable billing triggers fear of bill shock that throttles experimentation and daily adoption. Metering raw consumption also penalizes customers for retries, failed prompts, and verbose agent reasoning loops rather than charging for completed work, while exposing vendors to revenue deflation as underlying inference costs fall. In practice, sustainable AI platforms therefore converge on hybrid models that pair predictable base commitments with pooled usage allowances or outcome-based pricing.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Both models break because AI separates who uses the product from how much it costs to serve them and how much value they get from it.

Pure seat pricing assumes each user costs about the same and gets about the same value. That holds for traditional SaaS, where the marginal cost of a user is close to zero. With AI, every query uses inference compute. A few power users or automated agents can run up huge token bills on a single seat and wipe out the margin. AI also tends to replace or augment headcount, so a customer who gets more value often needs fewer seats, and revenue shrinks as success grows.

Pure usage pricing tracks cost but has its own problems. Bills are unpredictable, so finance and procurement teams resist them and budgeting gets hard. People ration their use, which slows adoption. Revenue swings make forecasting difficult. Raw units like tokens or API calls also map poorly to the business outcomes buyers care about, so pricing ends up tied to cost instead of value.

That's why most AI platforms now use hybrids: a platform or seat fee for predictability, bundled credits or usage tiers, overage charges, and sometimes outcome-based components.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Pure seat-based pricing breaks down in AI platforms because inference carries real, variable compute costs rather than the near-zero marginal costs of traditional SaaS. Heavy users or autonomous agents can quickly consume more compute than a flat per-user fee covers, eroding gross margins. Worse, because AI automates work and can reduce team headcount, tying revenue strictly to human seats penalizes the vendor precisely when the product delivers the most value.

Pure usage-based pricing fails from the opposite direction. Uncapped, variable bills create budget unpredictability and "bill shock," which enterprise procurement teams resist. Metering every prompt or agent run also introduces a taxi-meter effect that discourages employees from experimenting and adopting the tool. Finally, raw usage metrics like tokens rarely map cleanly to business outcomes: an inefficient prompt or a looping agent drives up costs without creating more value. In practice, most AI platforms adopt hybrid models—combining base subscriptions with usage pools or outcome tiers—to balance margin protection with predictable spend.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Pure usage-based pricing makes bills hard to predict. The same workflow can consume very different amounts of compute depending on the model, the length of the input, and how many steps an agent takes. Customers may limit adoption to avoid surprise bills, especially when units like tokens are hard to tie to business value.

Pure seat-based pricing gives customers a predictable bill, but seats are a poor proxy for how much work AI does. One employee can run agents that process thousands of tasks, while another barely uses the product. The vendor absorbs the cost of heavy usage, and customers pay for seats that may sit idle. Automation can even reduce the number of seats needed as the platform delivers more value.

That’s why many platforms combine a predictable subscription with included usage and charge for consumption beyond that allowance.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Pure usage-based pricing makes bills hard to predict, especially when two similar tasks can require very different amounts of computation. It can also charge more for a slow, inefficient result than for a quick, valuable one. Customers may ration use to avoid surprises, even when the platform is helping them.

Pure seat-based pricing gives customers a predictable bill, but a seat says little about how much AI work gets done. Two users paying the same fee can generate vastly different inference costs. And when an AI agent lets a smaller team do more work, the vendor can lose seat revenue even as the product delivers more value. A base fee with included usage and metered overages gives customers some predictability while letting revenue scale with heavier workloads.
